Nadia est soulagée. D’ici quelques semai: Nadia is relieved. In a few weeks, her daughter will finally have a teacher. Since the second week of school, dozens of substitutes have passed through her child’s Grade 1 classroom. “Every day it was someone new, and my daughter couldn’t even remember their name. One time, there was even a switch in the middle of the day,” says the mother.
Évidemment, cela a des répercussions. «: Naturally, this has consequences. “Academically, they’re barely moving forward, and my daughter also watches a lot of movies at school…
Bref, des périodes entières sont perdues: In short, entire periods are lost. And when I want to help her with her homework, I can see there’s no continuity from one teacher to the next,” she continues. The mother says “teacher,” but the people filling in aren’t always qualified staff. “I don’t blame the school; they’re sorry and everyone is doing their best. In fact, they just told us we’ll finally have a permanent teacher at the start of October.”
Cette enseignante quittera toutefois une: That teacher, however, will be leaving another class to fill the new position. Nadia is saddened that this is happening after a lockdown that was particularly hard on her family. “Let’s just say we needed a return to some normalcy and stability. We’re hoping it happens soon,” she sighs.

Pendant ce temps, de jeunes enseignants: Meanwhile, motivated, freshly graduated young teachers can’t enter the profession because they fall under the new Bill 21, which prohibits public service employees in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols. How many teachers are being kept out of schools as a result? The CAQ government tried to find out, but most school boards refused to do the count, arguing that doing so is in itself a discriminatory act. Counting students and graduates, the number of people affected in the field of teaching can nonetheless be estimated at a few hundred.
Nour Farhat est avocate. Ces jours-ci, e: Nour Farhat is a lawyer. These days, she is preparing for a major trial that will no doubt take up a good deal of media space in November. She will challenge Bill 21 in Superior Court on behalf of the Fédération autonome de l’enseignement (FAE) and its 45,000 teachers.
« Pouvoir agir directement dans un dossi: “Being able to act directly in a case where your own personal rights are being violated is incredible. It allows me to take back a bit of power over what happened to me,” says the lawyer, who wears a hijab and dreamed of being a Crown prosecutor. The case to be presented is truly astronomical in scale, pitting four plaintiffs against the government. About ten intervenors, for and against the law, will also take part in the trial. From a legal standpoint, the FAE’s position is clear: the law is unconstitutional. And that’s true even though the notwithstanding clause was used to adopt it.
Cette clause permet à un gouvernement d’: This clause allows a government to pass a law that contravenes certain provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, such as freedom of religion.
« Nous, on dit que la clause 33 [clause: “We’re saying that Section 33 [the notwithstanding clause] must be interpreted in light of the evolution of Canadian and international case law,” says Farhat. Another argument will focus on Section 6 of the Charter, which concerns mobility rights. According to the Charter, a Canadian citizen should be able to move and settle freely anywhere in the country, without constraint.
« Or, si par exemple un enseignant ou un: “Now, if for example a teacher affected by Bill 21 decides to go to Ontario for a year, then comes back to Quebec, she will no longer have the right to teach. In concrete terms, that’s a constraint that imprisons people, that prevents them from moving freely,” explains Farhat. As for Section 6, unlike the section on freedom of religion, it cannot be set aside by invoking the notwithstanding clause. All of this is much more than a debate among jurists. Nour Farhat has already heard heartbreaking stories from teachers governed by Bill 21.
« Nous allons d’ailleurs démontrer l’exi: “We are also going to demonstrate the existence of physical effects linked to discrimination. We’re talking about mental health, of course, but this law has outright negative physiological effects on those who endure this stress.” Farhat’s clients are teachers who already hold positions, and who are therefore protected by the “grandfather clause” (or acquired rights clause).
« Ce sont des gens qui peuvent rester en: “These are people who can keep their jobs, but who can’t move up, advance, relocate. They’re trapped and often feel humiliated in front of their colleagues. It creates two classes of teachers.”
Ichrak Nourel Hak est l’une des autres d: Ichrak Nourel Hak is another of the plaintiffs in the case. A recent education graduate, she now gives language support classes, hoping to one day have a classroom of her own. In the context of a shortage, she finds the situation doubly distressing and wants the government to reverse its position.
« S’il ne le fait pas pour ces personnes: “If it won’t do it for these people, who care deeply about education and students’ well-being, then let it at least do it for the students themselves, who deserve a quality education. The next generation deserves to thrive and to have access to the best resources,” says the young teacher.
Si on ignore le nombre exact d’enseignan: While the exact number of affected teachers is unknown, neither do we know what repercussions such legislation will have on future cohorts. For Derek Ross, executive director of the Christian Legal Fellowship, an organization of some 600 lawyers and law students in Canada, the numbers matter little anyway. The symbolism carries far more weight.
« En fin de compte, cela ne devrait pas: “At the end of the day, it shouldn’t be a question of numbers. Even if only one person is affected, it’s worth pursuing every legal avenue to the end,” says Ross. The Christian Legal Fellowship, it should be noted, was active from the very first hearings on the adoption of the legislation.
« Une loi comme celle-là risque d’avoir: “A law like this is likely to affect future students and their career choices, but also their sense of identity and their place in society,” the lawyer fears. In his view, Bill 21 reinforces negative associations with religion. And he adds that if the court challenge goes all the way to the Supreme Court, the impact on the ground will be felt for at least the next four years.
Fatima Ahmad est nouvellement diplômée e: Fatima Ahmad is a recent education graduate. Because she falls under Bill 21, she considered accepting a teaching position in Europe, before deciding to pursue further studies here while doing private tutoring with high school students. She confirms that they are worried about the future.
« Des jeunes filles musulmanes de 15, 16: “Muslim girls of 15 or 16 tell me they’re already ruling out certain careers for fear they won’t be able to get in. For young people, discrimination is becoming the norm,” reports the teacher.
Mais tous n’ont pas l’énergie ou l’espac: But not everyone has the energy or the headspace to fight. Safirah*, a Muslim teacher specializing in English as a second language, is barely aware that a major legal battle is taking shape. Exhausted, she has stopped following the case. “I feel a bit guilty, but this is my reality. I’m so tired…”
Quand la loi 21 est entrée en vigueur, S: When Bill 21 came into force, Safirah was teaching at a public school in Montréal. But because she was on a contract, it couldn’t be renewed. “The worst part is that I had offered to take off my hijab in class, in front of the children” – a compromise she wasn’t happy about, but was prepared to make.

The reasoning is based on the question of positions of authority. Taking off my religious symbol in front of the children should have been enough,” she says sadly.
Elle envisage aujourd’hui d’enseigner à: She is now considering teaching remotely for an Ontario school, an option that was just put to her and that she is slowly exploring. She uses the verb “explore” because she is no longer sure of anything.
« Honnêtement, je vais prendre le temps: “Honestly, I’m going to take the time to think. I’m going to spend time with my child. Maybe I’ll go back to school, or start my own small business. I have the luxury of not being a single mother with heavy financial responsibilities. I know others aren’t that lucky…” acknowledges Safirah.
La pénurie d’enseignants ne date pas d’h: The teacher shortage is nothing new, but the COVID-19 pandemic has certainly made the problem worse. While some teachers have decided to take early retirement, others are at risk and must work remotely. Right now, the situation is so critical that schools are hiring unqualified staff to run classrooms.
Parfois même en privant de services des: Sometimes they even do so by depriving students with special needs of services. For instance, the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal (CSSDM) is considering using remedial education specialists to teach full-time in classrooms, thereby depriving children with learning difficulties of the one-on-one support they need to succeed.
Pour pallier le manque, le gouvernement: To fill the gap, the government has also put in place a special measure to encourage retired teachers to come back and lend a hand.
Ces derniers pourront gagner jusqu’à 412: They will be able to earn up to $412 a day, compared with the usual maximum of $212, without any penalty to their pension benefits. The people interviewed in preparing this article are unanimous: the school year has barely begun, and it is already gruelling.
